title: 2 Chronicles 26:16–23
context: At the height of his strength, Uzziah's heart is lifted up, and he enters the temple to burn incense, a task reserved for the priests. Azariah the priest and eighty priests resist him. As Uzziah rages with censer in hand, leprosy breaks out on his forehead. He is hurried out, lives in a separate house until his death, and is cut off from the LORD's house while Jotham governs. This expands 2 Kings 15:5–7, which records the leprosy without giving its cause.

verses.text: But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up, so that he did corruptly and he trespassed against the LORD his God, for he went into the LORD’s temple to burn incense on the altar of incense.
verses.arminianNotes: "When he was strong, his heart was lifted up," and he went into the temple to burn incense. Arminian readers see pride freely embraced, leading a blessed king to overstep God's boundaries.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the very strength God gave becomes the occasion of Uzziah's fall. Pride turns blessing into presumption, and the king trespasses against the LORD his God.

verses.text: Azariah the priest went in after him, and with him eighty priests of the LORD, who were valiant men.
verses.arminianNotes: Azariah the priest and eighty valiant priests go in after him. Arminian readers note the courage of the priests in confronting a powerful king, faithful to their charge over the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the priests act to guard the holiness of God's house. Their courage shows faithfulness to God above loyalty to the king.

verses.text: They resisted Uzziah the king, and said to him, “It isn’t for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have trespassed. It will not be for your honor from the LORD God.”
verses.arminianNotes: The priests tell him, "It isn't for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD," and urge, "Go out of the sanctuary." Arminian readers see a clear warning, offering the king the opportunity to withdraw before judgment falls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the law assigned incense to Aaron and his sons (Exodus 30:7; Numbers 18:7). Both traditions see shared ground: God's worship is to be offered in his appointed way.

verses.text: Then Uzziah was angry. He had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and while he was angry with the priests, the leprosy broke out on his forehead before the priests in the LORD’s house, beside the altar of incense.
verses.arminianNotes: Uzziah grows angry, and while he rages with the censer, leprosy breaks out on his forehead. Arminian readers note that his anger at the warning, rather than repentance, precedes the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's judgment appears in the very place of the trespass, "beside the altar of incense." The king's presumption is answered immediately and visibly.

verses.text: Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked at him, and behold, he was leprous in his forehead; and they thrust him out quickly from there. Indeed, he himself also hurried to go out, because the LORD had struck him.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests see his leprosy and thrust him out, and he hurries out himself "because the LORD had struck him." Arminian readers note that the proud king is humbled at once.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator credits the LORD directly. Uzziah himself now hurries from the place he had insisted on entering, recognizing God's hand.

verses.text: Uzziah the king was a leper to the day of his death, and lived in a separate house, being a leper; for he was cut off from the LORD’s house. Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people of the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Uzziah is a leper until his death, lives in a separate house, and is "cut off from the LORD's house" while Jotham governs. Arminian readers see the lasting cost of a single proud act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 15:5, which simply says "the LORD struck the king." The Chronicler supplies the cause, and the two accounts are allowed to complement each other without forcing them together.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Uzziah's acts were written by "Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz." Arminian readers note that a prophet recorded his reign, though this writing is not otherwise preserved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Isaiah 6:1 dates the prophet's vision to "the year that King Uzziah died," consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 15:7.

verses.text: So Uzziah slept with his fathers; and they buried him with his fathers in the field of burial which belonged to the kings, for they said, “He is a leper.” Jotham his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: He is buried in the field of burial belonging to the kings, "for they said, 'He is a leper.'" Arminian readers note that even in death his leprosy sets him apart, a sober reminder of the cost of presumption.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 15:7 says he was buried with his fathers in David's city. The Chronicler adds the separation because of his leprosy; the difference in detail is noted, not harmonized.
